issues.description_html:
Problem/Motivation

We are in the process of deprecating jQuery UI in core. jQueryUI dialog is among the components that need to be removed/replaced.
This is a long term effort going back to Drupal 9, #3067261: [Plan] Remove jQuery UI components used by Drupal core and replace with a set of supported solutions.

The OpenJS Foundation lists jQuery UI as an Emeritus project in https://openjsf.org/projects/ which is described as:

Emeritus projects are those which the maintainers feel have reached or are nearing end-of-life

This issue was originally proposed as specifically looking for a polyfill. However, both the browser landscape and Drupal core have changed significantly since this issue was opened thirteen years ago. Today, all browsers support <dialog>. The only remaining lack is that Safari does not yet support the closedby property. In core we now have htmx, which is updated to v.4 for D12.

Proposed resolution

  1. Add a web component enhanced dialog as a single directory component.
  2. Add wrapper formats to render default, modal and off-canvas dialogs for processing by HTMX using the new hx-partial custom tag.
    • Insert dialog and side-positioned off-canvas div just before the end of the body.
    • Insert top-positioned off-canvas div just before the main canvas wrapper so that the main content is pushed down naturally.
    • The HtmxDialogRenderer detects a class query parameter on the request. This value is passed to the SDC and added to the dialog markup.
  3. Add an inbound path processor that takes a path /htmx/dialog/{type}/{path} and transforms it to /{path}?_wrapper_format="drupal_htmx_dialog.{type}"

Remaining tasks

Ready for review

User interface changes

This is an api level change.

API changes

Dynamic dialogs will now be created by a GET request to /htmx/dialog/{type}/{path} where {path} is the Drupal path that returns the markup which should appear in the dialog. Such requests are effected using HTMX trigger and request attributes.

Data model changes

jQuery UI Dialogs had a lot of options. The initial htmx solution offers dialog type and additional classes as options.

Release notes snippet

comments.body_html:
All existing jQuery UI Dialog JS plus its dependencies:

  • jquery.ui.dialog.js: 19,981 bytes
  • jquery.ui.core.js: 8,195 bytes
  • jquery.ui.widget.js: 15,069 bytes
  • jquery.ui.button.js: 11,821 bytes
  • jquery.ui.draggable.js: 31,128 bytes
  • jquery.ui.mouse.js: 4,561 bytes
  • jquery.ui.position.js: 15,676 bytes
  • jquery.ui.resizable.js: 27,400 bytes

For a total of 133,831 bytes or 130.7 KiB.

Then there's the CSS too:

  • jquery.ui.dialog.css: 1,304 bytes
  • jquery.ui.core.css: 1,468 bytes
  • jquery.ui.theme.css: 17,520 bytes
  • jquery.ui.button.css: 2,541 bytes
  • jquery.ui.resizable.css: 1,207 bytes

For a total of 24040 bytes or 23.5 KiB.

That's >150 KiB … for showing a dialog! Note that almost nothing in Drupal core uses jQuery UI, so it's extremely likely that we'd indeed be loading >150 KiB just for showing a dialog. Even if we'd be using it on all pages, 150 KiB is ridiculous. It's not acceptable, performance-wise.

(And note that I'm only looking at the jQuery UI dependencies, there's also the dependencies on jQuery, drupal.js, debounce.js and displace.js, which I'm not even counting because 1) most of those would be loaded already anyway, 2) most of those we'd probably continue to need after implementing nod_'s proposal.)

comments.author: andrewmacpherson
comments.body_html:
I tested the demo at https://demo.agektmr.com/dialog/ using Chrome 74 and Firefox 66. With Firefox, the page displays a message that the polyfill mode is being used.

I noticed a difference in the escape key behaviour, compared to jQueryUI dialog demos at https://jqueryui.com/dialog/

jQueryUI dialogs can be dismissed with the escape key, regardless of whether they are invoked with the modal: true option, so long as focus is within the dialog.

The GoogleChrome/dialog-polyfill demo differs from this. Pressing escape only dismisses dialogs which have been opened with showModal(); it doesn't dismiss the dialog which was opened with show().

As I read the HTML5.2 rec., user-agents aren't required to provide the escape key behaviour at all. It's a suggested behaviour ("may") for dialogs on the "pending dialog stack", which as far as I can tell only means dialogs which have been opened using showModal(). The HTML5.2 rec doesn't mention the pending dialog stack in the steps for the show() method. So it looks like the escape key behaviour in GoogleChrome/dialog-polyfill is comformant with the HTML 5.2 rec.

However it is different from the behaviour we currently get from jQueryUI.dialog, so we may risk an accessibility regression from what we have now. Non-modal dialogs are used in Drupal, notably the token browser dialog from contrib. I think all our dialogs currently have a close button at the top, which would mitigate the lack of the escape key behaviour (worth confirming though). Some uses of off-canvas dialog can be considered non-modal too, in that they don't prevent mouse interaction with buttons outside the dialog.

Aside: the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices recommend the escape key behaviour for modal dialogs. Note that non-modal dialogs aren't mentioned there at all; earlier drafts did include them, but they were removed because there were some issues which didn't get consensus in the WAI community. I don't recall what it said about the escape key behaviour for non-modal dialogs. FWIW, my view is that when focus is inside a non-modal dialog, the escape key should dismiss the dialog.

Leaving the needs accessibility review tag in place for now. There are other dialog polyfill libraries which can be reviewed.

comments.author: bnjmnm
comments.body_html:
Some findings on a11y-dialog from #3071552: Replace jQuery UI dialog with a supported dialog library

  • <summary> is not considered a focusable element - also an issue with jQueryUI. Also missing <embed> (it is confusing because there cab be focusable<details>without <summary>, but as long as <summary> is listed as a focusable element, focus will be properly trapped within <details>, even if it does not have summary.
  • Would require a separate library to be resizable. Technically jQueryUI also requires this, but it's part of the same suite
  • Doesn't look like there's a mechanism to elegantly pass in configuration options that would make it possible to have different styles/types of dialogs and settings like height and width. I was able to kind of implement this behavior by removing the creation of #drupal-modal-wrapper on init (which probably introduces other problems), so the attributes of the triggering element can be passed on to attributes in the dynamically created dialog Drupal.AjaxCommands.prototype.openDialog so dialogs can be styled differently. I found additional evidence that suggests this is possible - but some of the other issues still make this a not-ideal option.
  • There is no way to make elements outside of the dialog interactable while the dialog stays open, such as how it is used in layout builder. The a11y-dialog docs defines the difference of modal from a standard dialog as
    By default, a11y-dialog behaves as a dialog: it is closable with the ESC key, and by clicking the backdrop. However, it is possible to make it work like a “modal”, which would remove these features.
  • Expanding on the above point, that definition of modal includes preventing close when the escape key is pressed. This is technically a valid implementation, but would differ from Drupal's jQueryUI implementation, which allows close on escape with all dialog types.

comments.body_html:
I'm providing a patch that's more work-in-progress than I'd typically upload. Seeing how the jQueryUI issues are moving quickly and I'll be offline for at least a week, I wanted to make sure this was available so no work was duplicated.

The attached patch uses a native dialog when available. Browsers without native dialogs currently get a console.log().

Most of the work done was replicating the behavior of jQueryUI, so anything defined in a PHP render array or config yml will result in the same dialog. This patch already has Layout Builder off-canvas dialogs working near-identically to jQueryUI. Modals also largely work, but positioning hasn't been implemented yet. It'll still take some work (resize hasn't been implemented at all yet...), but replacing jQueryUI dialog is more feasible than I initially thought. Since dialog now has to work with native and a library equally, it's easier to swap libraries if needed.

It's still necessary to find a library to support browsers that don't have native dialog. The two major requirements of the library are:

  • It needs to be possible to open/close dialogs via Javascript. It can't rely on being coupled with buttons or other UI elements.
  • It needs to support non-modal dialogs (i.e. there has to be the option for the entire page to be interactable even when the dialog is open)

Although it would be nice, I the library doesn't necessarily need to be a11y focused - providing the accessibility capabilities via Drupal should not require much additional effort, and some of this was necessary to accommodate native dialogs. Here's some of the libraries reviewed so far
Nopes:
Tingle - https://robinparisi.github.io/tingle/ : modal only
Micromodal https://micromodal.now.sh/ : modal only
Jquery Modal https://github.com/kylefox/jquery-modal : modal only
Vex https://github.com/HubSpot/vex : modal only
Rmodal - https://rmodal.js.org/ : modal only
Van11y dialog https://van11y.net/downloads/modal/demo/index.html - no way to open/close via JS, it's all tied to input elements.

Maybes
Nyro modal (jquery) http://nyromodal.nyrodev.com/ : Meets the requirements but hasn't been updated since 2014.
JqModal http://jquery.iceburg.net/jqModal/#where : Meets the requirements and even has a companion resize library. Hasn't been updated since 2016

comments.author: bnjmnm
comments.body_html:
#23These are good questions and I'm glad they're being asked early in the process!

#23.1

I believe if a library misses requirement #1 [[Able to open/close dialogs via Javascript. It can't rely on being coupled with buttons or other UI elements.]] . It will always be possible to add that feature. I don't believe this is a big feature request.

This functionality is currently part of jQueryUI dialog and is key to how the dialog:beforecreate and dialog:aftercreate events work. If there's a way to preserve these events without the ability to trigger open/close via JS, I am very interested in knowing as it would make things easier.

function openDialog(settings) {
      settings = $.extend({}, drupalSettings.dialog, options, settings);
      // Trigger a global event to allow scripts to bind events to the dialog.
      $(window).trigger('dialog:beforecreate', [dialog, $element, settings]);
      $element.dialog(settings);
      dialog.open = true;
      $(window).trigger('dialog:aftercreate', [dialog, $element, settings]);
    }

    function closeDialog(value) {
      $(window).trigger('dialog:beforeclose', [dialog, $element]);
      $element.dialog('close');
      dialog.returnValue = value;
      dialog.open = false;
      $(window).trigger('dialog:afterclose', [dialog, $element]);
    }

This functionality also means that native dialogs and library-provided dialogs can largely use the same set of JavaScript. It's a dozen lines of additional code vs. potentially hundreds.

#23.2

Shouldn't accessibility be also a major requirement in usage?

Having the dialog be accessible is very important. It's not listed as a must have of the library as it's not particularly difficult to fill in accessibility gaps on the Drupal end (in fact, Drupal does a better job of constraining focus than even the accessibility-focused libraries) If there are multiple options that meet the must-have requirements, the more accessible option will certainly be chosen.

comments.author: andrewmacpherson
comments.body_html:
Can someone explain requirement #1, preferably with an example of where this behaviour is already being used, or a use-case where we might want to use this in future?

Dialogs open as a result of a user interaction. If they open without a user interaction, that's likely to be a failure of WCAG SC 3.2 5 "Change on request". The reason is that focus moves to a dialog when it opens, and that counts as a "change of context" for purposes of WCAG. If we have any instances of dialogs appearing without being a direct result of a specific user interaction, we should review those.

I think that requirement #1 is about situations where a user action may OR may not need a follow-on action from the user, depending on business logic. For example there are issues which propose using dialogs for the confirmation step in entity deletion operations (currently these are a redirection to a confirmation page). Have I understood this correctly?

UPDATED: Consider a situation like this...

  1. User presses a button to do something, which sends an AJAX request.
  2. The server-side logic looks at the request and decides that this is dangerous so needs a confirmation dialog.
  3. The server sends back an AJAX response containing a Command to show a confirmation dialog.
  4. The dialog would be programatically opened via JS, which isn't an event listener for any button.
  5. The dialog appears, gains focus, and is recognized by assistive tech.

This situation would pass WCAG "Change on request" IMO. The dialog appeared as clear consequence of a user pressing a button, even though the dialog was instantiated using requirement #1, and the decision to display the dialog was governed by business logic.

Note that messages which pop up as notifications are not dialogs, and shouldn't use a dialog element or role.

If we have any instances of dialogs appearing without being a direct result of a specific user interaction, we should review those.
I think that requirement #1 is about situations where a user action may OR may not need a follow-on action from the user, depending on business logic. For example there are issues which propose using dialogs for the confirmation step in entity deletion operations (currently these are a redirection to a confirmation page). Have I understood this correctly?
UPDATED: Consider a situation like this...
User presses a button to do something, which sends an AJAX request.
The server-side logic looks at the request and decides that this is dangerous so needs a confirmation dialog.
The server sends back an AJAX response containing a Command to show a confirmation dialog.
The dialog would be programatically opened via JS, which isn't an event listener for any button.
The dialog appears, gains focus, and is recognized by assistive tech.
This situation would pass WCAG "Change on request" IMO. The dialog appeared as clear consequence of a user pressing a button, even though the dialog was instantiated using requirement #1, and the decision to display the dialog was governed by business logic.
Note that messages which pop up as notifications are not dialogs, and shouldn't use a dialog element or role.

comments.author: andrewmacpherson
comments.body_html:
How many non-modal dialogs does core have?

I'm aware there are used in contrib. Notably, the token module uses one for the "browse available tokens" feature.

If requirement #2 is a sticking point, I suppose there's no hard requirement that modal and non-modal dialogs have to use the same underlying library?

I suspect the reason we're not finding much support for non-modal dialogs, is that they are actually very rare in web applications. I've often spoken with web developers who have never even heard of the concept of a non-modal dialog. Even among desktop applications, they are pretty uncommon, and are sometimes conflated with concepts like "dockable/floating toolbars", "palette", or "inspector".

Non-modal dialogs in web applications have been rather problematic for accessibility. A non-modal dialog pattern was included in an early draft of the ARIA Authoring Practices, but it was removed due to numerous problems which couldn't find a consensus. The main sticking point was how to locate them, when you aren't inside one. Dialogs aren't landmark regions, and are not required to have headings (ours do). In desktop applications, dialogs are easier to locate, since they are real windows. (Non-modal dialogs sometimes use a special palette/inspector window type with a standard keyboard command to locate them.)

Personally, I think it's worth reviewing our use of non-modal dialogs. Custom landmark regions may be more appropriate. Still, that doesn't help us with the current problem of replacing the jQuery UI library in a backwards-compatible way.

The list of libraries tested added to the summary in #22 overlooked GoogleChrome/dialog-polyfill which I reviewed in #12. I recall I was reasonably impressed with it at the time, but it could do with a more thorough API review perhaps.

I've also taken a look at the dialogs from dequelabs/pattern-library. It only aims to address modal dialogs by the look of it. It misses requirements 1 and 2, and I'm not sure how to evaluate requirement 3. I dug around the code to look at available methods. It's an interesting component accessibility-wise, but it doesn't attempt to be a polyfill for the HTML dialog element. It has interesting code to handle aria-hidden on elements outside the dialog, to prevent a screen reader finding them in browse mode.

This is all great feedback, lets see what I can help with...
#25

Can someone explain requirement #1, preferably with an example of where this behaviour is already being used, or a use-case where we might want to use this in future?

I'm not aware of any instances where dialogs open without user interaction, that is a very reasonable concern. This requirement makes it possible to trigger the events dialog:beforecreate dialog:aftercreate dialog:beforeclose dialog:afterclose, which are currently triggered anytime a dialog is opened/closed. These events are used by Ckeditor, Settings Tray, Toolbar, Layout Builder and Media Library. A common use for these is to add/remove classes on specific elements when a dialog is opened/closed and to trigger resizing.
A specific example I recently worked on can be found in Layout Builder. When a dialog is open that is specific to a block or section, that block/section is highlighted so it's clear what part of the layout is being configured. This is implemented by leveraging the dialog:aftercreate event, which pulls a data attribute from the dialog that indicates the element that needs to be highlighted.

#26

How many non-modal dialogs does core have?

This is certainly a good thing to know when gauging the importance of non-modal dialogs.
The UI for both Layout Builder and Settings Tray make extensive use of off-canvas dialogs, which are non-modal. I believe all uses of non-modal dialogs in core are via off-canvas, but I'm not 100% sure on that. If that's the case, it might be possible to implement off-canvas in a way that does not require a dialog library and (despite the overhead) worth exploring if there are no good options that meet requirement #2.

#26

Personally, I think it's worth reviewing our use of non-modal dialogs. Custom landmark regions may be more appropriate. Still, that doesn't help us with the current problem of replacing the jQuery UI library in a backwards-compatible way.

comments.body_html:
Created an issue that surfaced from the work happening in this one: #3082602: Remove transform rule from css_disable_transitions_test

The animation-disabling in Javascript tests is necessary for dialog tests to work consistently. These tests include disabling transform:, which causes a problem: the positioning for these new dialogs is managed by PopperJS, which uses transform: for placement. When animations are disabled (necessary for dialog tests), this can also result in parts of a dialog being out of viewport, and the test failing as a result.

For this issue to land, either #3082602 will need to be committed, or the patch in this issue will need to add a way of making transforms work in Javascript tests while other animations are disabled.

comments.author: bnjmnm
comments.body_html:
This is essentially a start-from-scratch based on steps I had to take in similar JS issues.

Unlike my prior attempt, this implementation is built to backwards compatible with all uses in core (and potentially contrib), and they are implemented in a manner that makes it possible to have the "new" dialog functionality live in an experimental module. The changes are currently in misc/dialog.es6.js so all tests run with this dialog implementation, but it can be moved to a module easily. There are a few other changes outside of dialog.es6.js, but they are ones that will also work fine with the jQueryUI implementation. Without some level of jQueryUI BC, the changes needed for dialogs (particularly off-canvas) to work from D9-D10 would be really unreasonable.

Also, my earlier patches would be near-impossible to review. This patch implements dialogs as a class so it's much easier to assess scope (it's still an enormous patch, but it should make far more sense to a reviewer).

Here are some remaining tasks and other bits of info:

  • Need to add focus trap on dialog open. Waiting on the RTBC issue #3113649: Remove drupal.tabbingmanager's jQueryUI dependency to land before doing this as it will likely change how this would be implemented.
  • The resizable functionality is still coming from jQueryUI. I haven't found a good alternative to jQueryUI resizable, and haven't yet explored the level of effort for a custom implementation. jQueryUI resizable is very complex, but it's possible much of the complexity isn't needed for core.
  • Draggable is not yet implemented, but I could not find any uses of draggable being enabled in core so I'm not yet sure if it's even needed
  • Positioning is complete enough to work fine in all core uses, but needs more attention before I could comfortably say it'll support contrib without a problem.
  • Several of the functions in this new Drupal.Dialog class are mimicing what jQuery UI dialog does, to the point where it's very possible there's lingering jQuery UI cruft that can be removed. In other words, this is still kind of ugly... but it's a dialog solution that supports core BC (that includes off canvas!), takes advantage of native dialogs, and has an added feature of returning focus to the opening element when a dialog closes.

comments.author: bnjmnm
comments.body_html:
Native dialog has been the approach as of ~3 years ago since I posted #18. It does sound like the polyfill may not ultimately be necessary because, let's face it, this is very unlikely to happen in 9.x.

The biggest hurdle is that core and contrib makes heavy use of the larger jQuery UI API such as events, draggability and resizability. There are not convenient native equivalents for those so we have to figure out ways to deprecate/BC/provide equivalents and other things to avoid breaking existing sites with the change.

There's also a markup backwards compatibility concern as a native dialog uses the <dialog> element, and Drupal core dialogs use <div> and there are styles, tests and JavaScript that rely on that assumption.

comments.author: nod_
comments.body_html:
Very cool to see work on this again!

  1. - The existing Drupal.dialog.showModal() and the native showModal() function have the same name, which gets slightly confusing.

    That was intended, sort of like there shouldn't be an intermediate API between Drupal and the dialog API. Drupal.dialog() should just return the native dialog DOM element. The return of the Drupal.dialog() function was made to mimick the native dialog DOM API. So something along the lines of the following should be enough: 

    Drupal.dialogNative = function () {
  return createDialog(element, settings);
}

    We can figure out events later (if needed), maybe we won't need them since we'll need to call attachbehaviors somehow on the dialog contents and contrib should not need to worry whether the content is in a modal or on a page. We had to do that before since jQuery has a lot of options that can be set, but that is not the case for native dialogs.

  2. - showModal() and show() seem to be doing mostly the same thing, just one with and one without backdrop? What did I miss?

    yep, same-ish. When openning a modal the rest of the content is not supposed to be "interactable": https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#blocked-by-a-mod...

  3. - Atm I've just set app/core/lib/Drupal/Core/Render/MainContent/DialogRenderer.php and app/core/lib/Drupal/Core/Render/MainContent/ModalRenderer.php to use the new native library but if we want both in parallel, this probably needs another solution. Too backend-y for me.

    That's ok, just need a way to test things out for now :)

  4. - Currently ajax response data is just put out again as is, this probably needs some checks.

    see the original Drupal.AjaxCommands.prototype.openDialog function. it uses the insert command to add html to the dialog so that behaviors are run automatically and all.

  5. - There's currently nothing for focus, tabbable, or the whole button change thing, I assume we need some of that back in.

    I'd test as-is for now. Seem like the focus is handled automatically by browsers and set it back to the triggering element when closing, probably nothing too bad to fix. As for buttons as long as the code is supposed to change existing form submit buttons it should work as-is. Views UI might give some trouble but we'll see when we get there.

comments.author: finnsky
comments.body_html:
Hello all!

I want to propose another approach that seems reasonable to me.
One of the main problems with the current implementation of the dialog in Drupal is the strong binding to jQueryUI styles and markup. This leaves the developer with few options, such as changing the order of dialog elements or adding new elements to the markup.

Currently, browser support for Web Components is the same as Drupal. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components

This way we can create a web component drupal-dialog which will
1. Create events when opening and closing.
2. Have an extremely flexible template, easily customizable via Drupal.theme.dialogTemplate
3. Support custom CSS properties
4. Save element styles in dialog slots. Example with claro buttons: https://gyazo.com/b8cb363cb5854415f0b023dcbf5d7fd1

This merge request is quite crude, but it does give some insight into the future benefits of this approach.

Currently tested is the confirmationDialog for changing the text format on the node edit page. For the test, add content to restricted HTML and change the format to basic. https://gyazo.com/e7a6f36d8b8e96e0f7719efdbeddfed9

Please review, Thanks!

comments.author: grevil
comments.body_html:
OK, to summarize the current state of this issue, it seems, that we agreed on using the native "dialog" element through adding an additional js library called "dailogNative". And slowly but surely deprecated the use of the jquery "dialog" library in the future. @TinaRey created a first draft with many of the required changes implemented ( see MR !4187, great work btw!). @catch and @larowlan agree with that approach in #78 and #79 respectively, and many others suggest a similar approach.

MR !397 by @bnjmnm and @_node is quite impressive but replaces the library instead of adding a new one, which could lead to problems for contrib modules, since we do not have a proper deprecation warning in place. But, we might be able to use some of the code from it :MR !4187.

The web-component approach by @finnsky also looks very promising. But should be added on top of the native dialogue library in a follow-up issue (if I understood that correctly).

I guess we can close these two MRs then for visibility’s sake and solely focus on MR !4187.

Reposting questions by @TinaRey in comment #83

  • The existing Drupal.dialog.showModal() and the native showModal() function have the same name, which gets slightly confusing.
  • showModal() and show() seem to be doing mostly the same thing, just one with and one without backdrop? What did I miss?
  • Atm I've just set app/core/lib/Drupal/Core/Render/MainContent/DialogRenderer.php and app/core/lib/Drupal/Core/Render/MainContent/ModalRenderer.php to use the new native library but if we want both in parallel, this probably needs another solution. Too backend-y for me.
  • Currently ajax response data is just put out again as is, this probably needs some checks.
  • There's currently nothing for focus, tabbable, or the whole button change thing, I assume we need some of that back in.
  • Needs tests
  • Needs styling

A few of these questions were already answered by @_node in #85 shortly after. So let's get to it! :)

comments.body_html:
Alright everyone, so based on the work done by @TinaRey and inspired by the jquery dialog adapter:"dialog.core.es6.js" by @bnjmnm. I worked on a contrib module the last couple of days, which "bridges" all existing Drupal.dialog() calls to use the new dialogNative library, called Dialog Native. It is still very much in a very early alpha stage and needs major testing, but creating dialog links such as:

<a class="use-ajax" 
    data-dialog-options="{"width":400}" 
    data-dialog-type="modal" 
    href="/node/1">
    First article displayed in modal dialog.
</a>

And the examples by @TinaRey:

editor: on a wysiwyg field, change the text format between basic_html and full_html
field_ui: on a content type, manage fields and attempt to delete one
in both cases, a native dialog should pop up, and the buttons should work

Already work. Although stuff like the off_canvas library is unfortunately broken, so no proper layout_builder for now...

Eventually, we could work on the module together, until it is solid, and we are able to merge large parts into core! I can also give out maintainer ship to speed things up, if necessary! Also I am very much in favour of a dedicated slack channel. Switching out the native dialog element with implementations of the popup API mentioned by @cosmicdreams, shouldn't be a problem, but we should discuss, what benefits it would bring us!

comments.author: latent
comments.body_html:
dialog demo 4 web component
Here is another possible idea to consider. We could implement this very small and simple web component <drupal-dialog> that acts as a simple wrapper for a native dialog tag. It only uses simple light dom with the server controlling its contents. It just handles some light polyfill and handles calling showModal when required and removes the inserted dialog as soon as you close it.

Web Component Features
- <dialog open data-modal> opens as modal via showModal(), backdrop, focus trap, top-layer
- <dialog open> opens as non-modal via show(), page stays interactive
- <dialog> (no open) inserted closed, stays in DOM until opened externally
- data-persist on <drupal-dialog> survives close, DOM kept, commandfor can reopen
- without data-persist self-removes from DOM on close
- closedby="any" on <dialog> click-backdrop-to-close, native Chrome 133+/Firefox 136+, polyfilled for Safari
- disconnectedCallback cleans up when htmx deletes the element server-side, closes dialog if still open
- skipClose flag guards against Firefox async close event firing during the open to show()/showModal() upgrade
- id on <drupal-dialog> is the htmx slot address (hx-target, delete swap)
- id on inner <dialog> is the commandfor target (two ids required when both are needed)

Triggering dialogs with hx-action:

- a trigger button carries only hx-action="some/endpoint", no hx-target or hx-swap
- the server response owns the swap strategy via two <hx-partial> tags
- first partial: <hx-partial hx-target="#slot-id" hx-swap="delete"> removes any existing dialog in that slot
- second partial: <hx-partial hx-target="body" hx-swap="beforeend"> appends the new <drupal-dialog> to the end of body
- because the response contains only <hx-partial> tags, htmx skips the main target swap entirely and only processes the partials
- the PHP command class is the only place that knows the slot id, swap strategy, and whether the dialog is modal or not
- for server-driven close, return only the delete partial with no insert partial
- for validation round-trips on an already open dialog, return a single <hx-partial hx-target="#slot-id" hx-swap="outerMorph"> instead, which updates the existing element in place without closing it

comments.author: anybody
comments.body_html:
Re #148 that won't be simple to answer, but some ideas:
1. We need to ensure backwards-compatibility, so probably the old parameters (like with and height) need to be able to override the default? (Still they should never be required, defaulting to an responisive auto layout).
And we should be able to deprecate them in the future!
Maybe it makes sense to predefine some "layouts" through classes? (e.g. .w-full, w-80, ... or do nothing and leave this to the theme or layout system?)

2. Dialog SDC should allow passing all HTML dialog properties (open, Popover API HTML attributes, ...?) and while open might be special enough to be a custom SDC property, other attributes should just be added through the Attributes object IMHO.
2.1. dialog can have alertdialog role: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Referenc... - should that have special handling or also get added through Attributes where needed?

3. Besides that I think as much as possible should be left to CSS! The default sizing, modal styling, etc. is very well-placed in CSS and if we're able to add ID and classes on the <dialog> in the SDC (and later in UI), that should be very flexible and the very best option.

comments.author: thomas.frobieter
comments.body_html:
Having spent years wrestling with the Core Dialog as a theme developer, I would like to stress that the sizing of the modal should be handled using CSS alone. Today's CSS should provide us with everything we need, meaning JavaScript should no longer be required for sizing purposes.
In any case, I can't think of a situation right now where that would be necessary. At most, it might be needed for special cases where the user can resize the modal — if that were to be part of the core implementation, of course.

If width and height are still necessary properties, I would use it as max-width and max-height values (plus height: 100% and width: 100% to prevent the modal from shrinking).

If we look at major UI frameworks like Bootstrap, they use a bunch of standard sizes, which, in my opinion, should cover 95% of cases.

comments.author: thomas.frobieter
comments.body_html:
@mherchel Should we continue to use the ui-* classes for BC as we move things into the SDC?

IMO, the ui-* classes should be removed. That's the typical jQuery UI prefix, and it only causes confusion if it continues to be used without jQuery UI.

Looking at the CSS classes some things doesn't seem right to me yet.

Some of this is apparently for backward compatibility (especially the dialog-off-canvas classes), but if we can make a few more adjustments to the classes now, we may should do so.

  1. Use a reliable BEM block class (.dialog, .drupal-dialog, ...?)
  2. Use proper BEM element classes for the child elements, eg. .dialog-content should be .dialog__content (if .dialog becomes the block class)
  3. Formatter classes usally don't need the block class, nor the HTML element in the CSS selector. So it should be .dialog--narrow instead dialog.dialog--narrow
  4. Is .titlebar used outside the dialog context? If not, it should be .dialog__titlebar and .dialog__titlebar-close
  5. Consider using CSS custom properties for the sizing values (--dialog-width / --dialog-max-width, --dialog-height / --dialog-max-height). This makes it easier for themers to work with variables and it's a cleaner approach for the default sizing formatters too.

I was unable to create a test modal within my Drupal DDEV instance, so I could not check the current behaviour. However, in my experience, the most reliable approach for sizing dialogs is to use a width of 100% (to prevent shrinking), max-width/max-height, and flexbox justify-content/align-items, or margin: auto, to center it. However, the min/minmax approach might be better for a default 'auto sizing' if no specific size has been set.

comments.author: rkoller
comments.body_html:
This is an extended summary of a few comments of mine over in the #htmx channel in the Drupal Slack. I've played around for a little while with the dialog_renderer_test test module accessing /htmx-dialog-test-markup with MR16540 during and after the biweekly Slack meeting on the 8th of October (thread #3).

The general direction is already a significant improvement. In particular, adopting the dialog element instead of using a generic div element is improving the status quo on modern browsers tremendously. In manual testing the modal behaved correctly in regard to the aural interface in VoiceOver on macOS. Meaning, with the dialog modal expanded and with the rotor activated in VoiceOver on macOS, only the elements contained within the dialog element are included in the aural interface; every other element in the modal's "background" is getting excluded. Also, the tabbing order looks correct; the focus is only on focusable elements within the dialog modal and the browser window itself (Safari in my case), everything else is excluded from the tabbing order. It is also possible to close the modal by keyboard, either by pressing Escape or by pressing the Close button on the keyboard. All good in general - I've tested in Safari, Firefox, and Edge . There is a general checklist for dialog modals for EAA compliance, which is provided over here https://handreichungen.bfit-bund.de/accessible-uie/modaler_dialog.html#. Aside from that, there are few details to denote that might get improved:

  • On the element opening/expanding the dialog modal, there is no indication on the aural interface that pressing/clicking that element will open a dialog modal, which leads to a context shift. Therefore, a screenreader user is lacking situational awareness in that context. One way to mitigate this might be to add the aria-haspopup="dialog" attribute to the element responsible for triggering the opening/expansion of a dialog modal.
  • The dialog title is using an h2. The consensus for Drupal Core that was agreed on in the accessibility group for dialog modals was to use an h1 on dialog modals and using an h2 on non-dialog modals - see #3485202: Change the element wrapping the title in dialogs from span to heading element.
  • Out of the scope for the current issue is the question what to focus on when the dialog modal is getting expanded. For the examples in the test module, the Close button is getting into focus. Problem is, the first three examples only contain one h2, a short div containing the dialog content, and the Close button, but there are no additional form elements. But on which element to focus on right after the expansion of a dialog modal heavily depends on the given context, aka what is contained in the modal. That way there is no general way to say, "Let's always focus on the Close button" aka the only and/or first focusable element - in a few scenarios that might make it the appropriate choice, in other scenarios it might be the exact opposite. You have to simply ask yourself, would closing a modal be the top task a user wants to do right next after opening a dialog modal? Adrian Roselli illustrates a few potential different scenarios in the following blog post: https://adrianroselli.com/2025/06/where-to-put-focus-when-opening-a-moda.... Due to the fact that it is heavily context-dependent, the solution would probably stall the current issue, and therefore I am tempted to recommend opening a dedicated follow-up issue for discussing and solving that problem in a flexible manner.

As far as I understand at the moment, htmx is being used to open a dialog modal. I've wondered and already asked on Slack if it would be a reasonable step instead of using JavaScript for triggering the opening of a dialog modal to use the Invoker Commands API instead (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Invoker_Commands_API). The Invoker Commands API has been available in all major browsers for a while now (https://caniuse.com/?search=invoker+comm). That way the foundation of opening and closing of a dialog modal as well as the dialog element itself would be plain HTML, while the dynamic parts within a dialog modal same as certain compatibility edge cases could be covered by htmx/JavaScript?

Meaning, with the dialog modal expanded and with the rotor activated in VoiceOver on macOS, only the elements contained within the dialog element are included in the aural interface; every other element in the modal's "background" is getting excluded. Also, the tabbing order looks correct; the focus is only on focusable elements within the dialog modal and the browser window itself (Safari in my case), everything else is excluded from the tabbing order. It is also possible to close the modal by keyboard, either by pressing Escape or by pressing the Close button on the keyboard. All good in general - I've tested in Safari, Firefox, and Edge . There is a general checklist for dialog modals for EAA compliance, which is provided over here https://handreichungen.bfit-bund.de/accessible-uie/modaler_dialog.html#. Aside from that, there are few details to denote that might get improved:
On the element opening/expanding the dialog modal, there is no indication on the aural interface that pressing/clicking that element will open a dialog modal, which leads to a context shift. Therefore, a screenreader user is lacking situational awareness in that context. One way to mitigate this might be to add the aria-haspopup="dialog" attribute to the element responsible for triggering the opening/expansion of a dialog modal.
The dialog title is using an h2. The consensus for Drupal Core that was agreed on in the accessibility group for dialog modals was to use an h1 on dialog modals and using an h2 on non-dialog modals - see #3485202: Change the element wrapping the title in dialogs from span to heading element.
Out of the scope for the current issue is the question what to focus on when the dialog modal is getting expanded. For the examples in the test module, the Close button is getting into focus. Problem is, the first three examples only contain one h2, a short div containing the dialog content, and the Close button, but there are no additional form elements. But on which element to focus on right after the expansion of a dialog modal heavily depends on the given context, aka what is contained in the modal. That way there is no general way to say, "Let's always focus on the Close button" aka the only and/or first focusable element - in a few scenarios that might make it the appropriate choice, in other scenarios it might be the exact opposite. You have to simply ask yourself, would closing a modal be the top task a user wants to do right next after opening a dialog modal? Adrian Roselli illustrates a few potential different scenarios in the following blog post: https://adrianroselli.com/2025/06/where-to-put-focus-when-opening-a-moda.... Due to the fact that it is heavily context-dependent, the solution would probably stall the current issue, and therefore I am tempted to recommend opening a dedicated follow-up issue for discussing and solving that problem in a flexible manner.
As far as I understand at the moment, htmx is being used to open a dialog modal. I've wondered and already asked on Slack if it would be a reasonable step instead of using JavaScript for triggering the opening of a dialog modal to use the Invoker Commands API instead (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Invoker_Commands_API). The Invoker Commands API has been available in all major browsers for a while now (https://caniuse.com/?search=invoker+comm). That way the foundation of opening and closing of a dialog modal as well as the dialog element itself would be plain HTML, while the dynamic parts within a dialog modal same as certain compatibility edge cases could be covered by htmx/JavaScript?

I did some more testing and surfaced a few more problems. I am testing on macOS 26.7.1 on Safari 27.0, Firefox Developer Edition 160.0b1, and MS Edge 155.0.4283.62 with VoiceOver enabled.

@fathershawn: Not unrelated. SDCs are just a rather new thing in Drupal.

For performance reasons, GenerateThemeTest excludes /core/assets from the test codebase, see the blame. The SDC validation schema however lives in /core/assets/schemas, so mere discovery of an SDC such as this will inevitably produce a 500.
I'm not excluding an additional path, however. Rather I'm narrowing down the exclusion to /core/assets/vendor, so SDCs continue to work. 👍

I'll do a manual review now to see if the shiny new jQuery UI replacement already works as a smooth drop in or which changes we might want to make. Thanks for your incredible work!

comments.author: pancho
comments.body_html:
The HTMX SDC may absolutely land first, sure, if that's the preferred way.

Pro: Without the HTMX SDC landing in Core, we may not need the backend infrastructure even though a level of refactoring would improve the status quo as well.

Contra: Whenever we're introducing new architecture such as the HTMX SDC, we generally want to make sure it is immediately used so most issues are ironed out and there's proper testing. Plus: It seems obvious that your HTMX SDC is going to land as everybody wants to get rid of jQuery UI and all the awful glue code.

But probably there's an intermediate way:
Let's start rightaway with those parts that generate immediate return on investments and only leave those abstractions as a followup that wouldn't be needed without the HTMX SDC landing.

Also, the amount of BC breakage can be massively reduced. Obviously, once jQuery UI is removed, users may not use its specific features any longer. And custom code that depends on exactly the way jQuery UI and our glue code work, will have to change. That's unavoidable. But most breakage can be avoided.

Unfortunately I'm not yet on Drupal Slack. But once I find a bit time over the weekend, I will join the #htmx channel. See you there!

Form API 'item' elements should not use the 'for' attribute
issues.description_html:
Problem/Motivation

According to the HTML specification when using the "label" element the "for" attribute should only be used when the element you're labelling is "labelable". See: http://www.w3.org/html/wg/drafts/html/master/forms.html#the-label-element

Labelable elements are:
button
input (if the type attribute is not in the Hidden state)
keygen
meter
output
progress
select
textarea
form-associated custom elements

Steps to reproduce

  1. Install Drupal with the Standard profile.
  2. Visit /admin/config/media/file-system.
  3. Inspect the markup for "Public file base URL",

In addition to inspecting the markup, note the pointer as you hover over the text in Step 3.

Proposed resolution

  1. Add the property non_labelable to the Item element (Drupal\Core\Render\Element\Item).
  2. Add the variable tag to all versions of form-element-label.html.twig.
  3. In core/lib/Drupal/Core/Form/FormPreprocess.php, set that variable to label if the form element is labelable (and keep the existing markup). If not, then set tag to span, add an id attribute to it, and add an aria-describedby attribute to the wrapping <div>. (Since (1) applies only to Item elements, that is the only non-labelable form element.)

In future issues, we may add the non_labelable property to other form elements. In (3), the code just checks for the property, not the element type.

Remaining tasks

User interface changes

Here is the markup for the "Public file base URL" section: see the Steps to Reproduce. Both code snippets below use the Default Admin theme.

Before

<div data-drupal-wrapper-selector="edit-file-public-path" id="edit-file-public-path" class="js-form-item form-item js-form-type-item form-type--item js-form-item-file-public-path form-item--file-public-path">
            <label for="edit-file-public-path" class="form-item__label">Public file system path</label>
              sites/default/files
              <div id="edit-file-public-path--description" class="form-item__description">
      A local file system path where public files will be stored. This directory must exist and be writable by Drupal. This directory must be relative to the Drupal installation directory and be accessible over the web. This must be changed in settings.php
    </div>
  </div>

The <label> element has a for attribute referring to the wrapping <div>.

After

<div data-drupal-wrapper-selector="edit-file-public-path" id="edit-file-public-path" aria-describedby="edit-file-public-path--label" class="js-form-item form-item js-form-type-item form-type--item js-form-item-file-public-path form-item--file-public-path">
            <span id="edit-file-public-path--label" class="form-item__label">Public file system path</span>
              sites/default/files
              <div id="edit-file-public-path--description" class="form-item__description">
      A local file system path where public files will be stored. This directory must exist and be writable by Drupal. This directory must be relative to the Drupal installation directory and be accessible over the web. This must be changed in settings.php
    </div>
  </div>

The <label> element is replaced by a <span> element with an id attribute. The wrapping <div> refers to that element using aria-describedby.

Introduced terminology

None

API changes

None

Data model changes

None

Release notes snippet

N/A

Original report by specky_rum

According to the HTML specification when using the "label" element the "for" attribute should only be used when the element you're labelling is "labelable". See: http://www.w3.org/html/wg/drafts/html/master/forms.html#the-label-element

Labelable elements are:
button
input (if the type attribute is not in the Hidden state)
keygen
meter
output
progress
select
textarea

Currently the theme_form_element_label($variables) function takes no account of the type of the element it is labelling. As long as there's an ID for the element it adds this as the "for" attribute. This is done where it does this:

  if (!empty($element['#id'])) {
    $attributes['for'] = $element['#id'];
  }

The "for" attribute is not a required attribute so presumably we could just add an array of element names or Drupal form element types in this function to exclude the "for" attribute?

The reason this has come up is that a site we manage failed an accessibility check run by the Shaw Trust in the UK. The issue they raised was that there are labels without a corresponding element. In fact, they do have an element, it's just that it's a div. The specific example is a form created using the entityform module which includes a list of checkboxes. Now although that's a contrib module it uses the standard Drupal core field rendering code. An example of the resultant code for checkboxes is something like:

<div class="form-item form-type-checkboxes form-item-field-a3-posters-location-und">
  <label for="edit-field-a3-posters-location-und">Location </label>
 <div id="edit-field-a3-posters-location-und" class="form-checkboxes"><div class="form-item form-type-checkbox form-item-field-a3-posters-location-und-Adam-and-Eve-Street-car-park">
 <input id="edit-field-a3-posters-location-und-adam-and-eve-street-car-park" name="field_a3_posters_location[und][Adam and Eve Street car park]" value="Adam and Eve Street car park" class="form-checkbox" type="checkbox">  <label class="option" for="edit-field-a3-posters-location-und-adam-and-eve-street-car-park">Adam and Eve Street car park (2 sides; behind Grafton centre) </label>

</div>

The only problem with that code is that the label's "for" attribute refers to the id of a div which is not a "labelable" element.

We have got round this for the very specific instance of checkboxes by implementing theme_form_element_label($variables) in our theme but this is a very specific override and not appropriate to core. Our full override function is as follows (it will be extended to pick up other element types in future):

function theme_form_element_label($variables) {
  // run the regular theme function on it
  $output = theme_form_element_label($variables);
  
  // check if it's checkboxes
  if ($variables['element']['#type'] == 'checkboxes') {
    // if it is, strip out the "for" attribute
    $output = preg_replace('#\s(for)="[^"]+"#', '', $output);
  }
  return $output;
}

comments.author: David_Rothstein
comments.body_html:
I think this might still be relevant actually. Even if Drupal 8 fixed it for checkboxes and radios, is it still a problem for other elements?

We can't switch label to legend in Drupal 7 certainly, but simply leaving out the "for" attribute in these cases seems like it would be doable as a backport. However, would that really help accessibility - i.e. is pointing screen readers nowhere better than pointing them to a div? Seems like it might actually be worse...

Personally I've also come across this issue during automated accessibility scans of particular sites, but note #884846-39: Orphaned Labels Being Generated for Radios, Checkboxes & Items which suggests that this issue has "no real impact on users, only on testing tools". I used that as a justification not to bother fixing it on the site in question :)

I see the Forms API dealing with this properly on the Admin > Configuration > Text formats > Basic HTML page under "Enabled filters" when you inspect the code. Here's a code snippet:

<div id="filters-status-wrapper"><div id="edit-filters-status" class="js-form-item form-item js-form-type-item form-type-item js-form-item- form-item-">

comments.author: klonos
comments.body_html:
@katannshaw and @Amber Himes Matz admittedly this is a hard problem to fix, but at the same time I don't think that it can be marked as "works as designed".

To sum up the problem:

  • <label> elements should have a for attribute that points to an HTML id of a labelable element (see https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#the-label-element )
  • <div> elements are NOT labelable elements (see https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#category-label ), so they should not be pointed to via the for attribute (and not have a <label> to begin with).

So this for example, is NOT proper use of the label and for attribute:

<div id="edit-my-item" >
  <label for="edit-my-item">Test item </label>
  <div class="description">Test item description.</div>
</div>

After some quick research, the best suggestion I have found is to use a combination of a <span> and the aria-describedby attribute. Something like this for instance:

<div aria-describedby="label-for-div" >
  <span id="label-for-div">Test item </span>
  <div class="description">Test item description.</div>
</div>

Noting the following from https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attribut... :

  1. the aria-labelledby attribute is not appropriate, because it should only be used for interactive elements (which div s are NOT)
  2. the aria-describedby is not ideal either, since it should be used for a description (longer text) rather than a label (short text)

The purpose of aria-labelledby is the same as that of aria-label . It provides the user with a recognizable, accessible name for an interactive element.

The aria-labelledby and aria-describedby attributes both reference other elements to calculate text alternatives. aria-labelledby should reference brief text that provides the element with an accessible name. aria-describedby is used to reference longer content that provides a description.

Reopening this issue in order to figure out a proper solution to this, rather than haste to dismiss it.

comments.author: mgifford
comments.body_html:
So after looking at https://www.drupal.org/project/drupal/issues/3082011 I thought there were elements of @intrafusion's which should be pulled into this.

This consolidation adds on top https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/16464/diffs

1. Explicit `#non_labelable` metadata for wrappers like `#type => item`.
2. Programmatic association for non-labelable wrappers via:
- wrapper: `id="-wrapper"` + `aria-describedby="-label"`
- title: `-label">...` (or custom `#title_tag`)
3. Regression coverage proving the relationship (no invalid `label[for]` targeting `div`, no orphan title text).

Credit first: this approach builds directly on intrafusion's re-roll in #3082011 comment #16669292 (`3082011-22.patch`). Thank you, @intrafusion, for pushing the `#title_tag` + template simplification pattern forward.

#### 1. W3C / HTML spec compliance
Per HTML spec, `label[for]` is for labelable controls only (`input`, `select`, `textarea`, `button`, etc.). Pointing `for` at a `div` fails validation and creates noisy false positives in scanners.

#### 2. Accessible association via ARIA
Removing invalid `for` references is necessary, but not sufficient. We still need a programmatic relationship between wrapper and title for assistive tech.

This patch path does that by:
- marking elements as non-labelable (`#non_labelable => TRUE`),
- rendering wrapper ids as `-wrapper`,
- rendering title ids as `-label`,
- wiring wrapper `aria-describedby` to the title id.

So we get valid HTML and preserved accessibility semantics.

This is an AI generated consolidation, but made sense to me.

Per HTML spec, `label[for]` is for labelable controls only (`input`, `select`, `textarea`, `button`, etc.). Pointing `for` at a `div` fails validation and creates noisy false positives in scanners.
#### 2. Accessible association via ARIA
Removing invalid `for` references is necessary, but not sufficient. We still need a programmatic relationship between wrapper and title for assistive tech.
This patch path does that by:
- marking elements as non-labelable (`#non_labelable => TRUE`),
- rendering wrapper ids as `-wrapper`,
- rendering title ids as `-label`,
- wiring wrapper `aria-describedby` to the title id.
So we get valid HTML and preserved accessibility semantics.
This is an AI generated consolidation, but made sense to me.

#states not affecting visibility/requirement of managed_file
issues.description_html:
Problem/Motivation

Cannot affect the visibility or requirement of managed_file with states. Identical to #1118016: conditional visibility of a managed_file using #states attribute does not work so either the bug wasn't fully fixed before, or a regression happened at some point and broke this functionality.

With this definition:

$form['type'] = array(
  '#type' => 'select',
  '#options' => array(
    'video' => t('Video'),
    'audio' => t('Audio'),
    'post' => t('Text'),
  ),
);

$form['audio'] = array(
  '#type' => 'managed_file',
  '#title' => t('Audio File'),
  '#states' => array(
    'visible'  => array(':input[name="type"]' => array('value' => 'audio')),
    'required' => array(':input[name="type"]' => array('value' => 'audio')),
  ),
  '#upload_location' => 'public://',
  '#upload_validators' => array(
    'file_validate_extensions' => array('mp3 wac'),
    'file_validate_size' => array(1048576),
  ),
);

I expect the visibility of "audio" to change when changing the value of "type". What happens is "audio" remains visible and not required. Simply changing "managed_file" to "file" brings the expected behavior.

Steps to reproduce

1. Create a custom form with structure as above
2. Navigate to the form
Problems:
1. On page load the "audio file upload" option is shown, which should show up only on selecting the Audio option.
2. Mandatory asterix is not shown for audio file upload field when the Audio option is selected

Proposed resolution

Root cause: During porting of fix from 8.x to 9.x the bug seems to be introduced. In the
function template_preprocess_file_managed_file(&$variables) {
there
$variables['attributes'] = [];
is overridden.

Proposed fix: Conditionally override to ensure if that the attributes set for #states is not lost.

For the "required" capability of #states to work, the label has to be correctly set, so that the mandatory asterix can be set. The managed_file introduces a "upload" index. Set the #states to the "upload" index as the label refers to the this and not the original "audio" field.

Remaining tasks

User interface changes

API changes

Data model changes

Release notes snippet

comments.author: scott_euser
comments.body_html:
There appears to be two issues with the managed file. This is my understanding of it, but please correct me if I have it wrong.

The managed file input is loaded via ajax and appears within an 'ajax-wrapper' div
By the time it is loaded it appears that this bit of core/misc/states.js

Drupal.behaviors.states = {
  attach: function (context, settings) {
  }
};

which assigns the fields as Dependants of the triggering input (in this case the select) has already been run. The ajax loaded file_managed field is then not assigned as a Dependent. Because of that, when the 'state:visible' event is triggered, the ajax loaded file_managed is uneffected.

The 'data-drupal-states' attribute is not being added to the ajax loaded file_managed input
With a file input instead of file managed, a 'data-drupal-states' attribute is added to the input with json encoded settings specifying which element the Dependent is dependent upon and when it should be made visible. This information is not available in the ajax loaded element, so even if triggered the attach function (above) again, it wouldn't know how to handle this input.

Possible solution
Perhaps we can attach the data-drupal-states directly to the ajax-wrapper container so regardless of what happens within the file_managed, we can be sure the states are obeyed. I am not sure if that might have other unintended consequences so perhaps the above two issues need to be addressed independently.

comments.body_html:
I encountered this problem when creating a custom field widget where managed_file fields along others should be visible according to a select filed. Applying this patch made the whole custom field disappearing because states.js now changed the visibility of the entire fieldset. Because of state.js function $(e.target).closest('.js-form-item, .js-form-submit, .js-form-wrapper').toggle(e.value) the fieldset appeared als closest to the ajax-wrapper element. I discovered, that the upload element didn't had states by default. So for my needs, it was enough to add states to just the upload input element without the ajax wrapper, because states.js can still get the states of these elements and toggle them accordingly. I placed it right below the $element['upload'] definition, to keep it in line. Starting from line 303

        // The file upload field itself.
        $element['upload'] = [
            '#name'             => 'files[' . $parents_prefix . ']',

            '#title'            => t('Choose a file'),

            '#theme_wrappers'   => [],

            '#error_no_message' => true,
        ];
        if (!empty($element['#accept'])) {
            $element['upload']['#attributes'] = ['accept' => $element['#accept']];
        }

            $element['upload']['#states'] = $element['#states'];
        }

comments.author: piotrkonefal
comments.body_html:
The same issue seems to be occurring on Webforms. Conditional logic options based on state of `managed_file` field does not seem to work.
Steps to reproduce:

  1. Create a webform with a file field.
  2. In Webform configuration (Build > Elements section), choose 'Edit' option for 'Submit button(s)'.
  3. Switch to 'Conditions' tab.
  4. Set a condition as: Visible - If - File Field (is) - Filled
  5. Save webform settings.
  6. Go to the webform. Observe that submit button is hidden, based on configured condition.
  7. Upload a file - see that 'Submit' button is still NOT visible (but it should be)

There is a working workaround for that scenario:
1. Add custom webform handler and use it on affected webform.
2. Define alterForm() method and build conditional visibility there.
Example:

$form['elements']['actions']['#states'] = [
      'visible' => [
          '.webform-submission-activity-tasks-form :input[data-drupal-selector="edit-presentation-fids"]' => ['filled' => TRUE],
      ],
    ];

In terms of Webforms there is another issue I've caught which is related to this one. I've created a separate thread: https://www.drupal.org/project/webform/issues/3399906#comment-15308665

issues.description_html:
Follow-up to #2152217: Remove theme_form_required_marker() from the theme system - use CSS instead

Updated as of #165.

Problem/Motivation

3 years ago, in #2152217: Remove theme_form_required_marker() from the theme system - use CSS instead, the community decided to remove the star (*) used to indicate that a form field is required from the source code to add it from the CSS. Initially, the issue was just about converting the theme function to a Twig template but changed quickly. The purpose of this change was to simplify theming and improve accessibility. The thing is that, according to WCAG, this is not as accessible as we thought.

References:

  • WCAG 2.0 - 1.1.1 Non-text Content
  • F3: Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 due to using CSS to include images that convey important information
  • WCAG 2.0 - 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
  • Accessiweb 2.2 - Criterion 10.2 - [Bronze] On each Web page, is visible content still available when style sheets or images are disabled? (Accessiweb is the French accessibility standard)
  • F87: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 due to inserting non-decorative content by using :before and :after pseudo-elements and the 'content' property in CSS. [The latest version of this document says that it is obsolete.]

Steps to reproduce:

Standard cases
  1. Go to any page including a form with required fields (eg. /user/login)
  2. Disable CSS in your browser
With JavaScript states API

Note: This mimics the automated test.

  1. In settings.local.php, uncomment the line $settings['extension_discovery_scan_tests'] = TRUE;, or add that line to settings.php.
  2. Enable the form_test module.
  3. Go to form-test/javascript-states-form.
  4. Check the checkbox named "Checkbox trigger".
  5. Find the textfield named "Textfield required when checkbox trigger checked", and note the required marker (star / asterisk).
  6. Disable CSS.
  7. Find the textfield named "Textfield required when checkbox trigger checked" again.

Current result: the stars on field labels are absent and there is no other visual indication that the field is required

Expected result: there is still some visual indication about the status of the required field

Screenshots

With CSS Without CSS
Before patch
After patch

Proposed resolution

  1. Bring back markup, but use the string "(required)" instead of "*" (aka, an asterisk or star).
  2. Wrap the new markup in a span with both:
    • The hidden CSS class to avoid changing the current look of the existing sites.
    • aria-hidden to avoid screen readers to vocalize the content of the span, as it's already covered by the aria-required and HTML5 required attributes.
  3. Put that span inside form labels and other interactive elements to increase target size.
  4. Apply these changes to the following elements. In some cases this will result in duplication of the "(required)" string with the same on the child field labels, but this is acceptable.
    • All standard form element labels.
    • legend elements (inside fieldset).
    • summary elements (inside details).
    • The h4 element that precedes datetime fields.
    • The JavaScript states API (as a JavaScript theme function in core/misc/states.js).

    See options 1 and 2 below for details on the different proposed implementations.

  5. Update tests & add coverage as needed.

Implementation options

  • Option 1: Append the text in template files. https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/12981.
    This MR was RTBC until #156.
    @larowlan supports this option.     Option 2 was chosen in #174.
  • Option 2: Append the text in the PHP render chain. https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/15924.
    @catch, @smustgrave, @kentr support this option. @larowlan didn't report concerns with the code in the MR.
    Discussion starts at #154.

comments.author: mgifford
comments.body_html:
Thanks @DuaelFr - this is an interesting issue and one that we obviously didn't fully consider when making this change.

I think that part of this was the confidence that we are already providing a lot of semantic information for assistive technology users.

So in this case the semantics should be covered by both required="required" aria-required="true":
<input class="js-text-full text-full form-text required" data-drupal-selector="edit-title-0-value" id="edit-title-0-value" name="title[0][value]" value="" size="60" maxlength="255" placeholder="" required="required" aria-required="true" type="text">

It is also interesting that the text is a symbol '*' rather than a word like '(required)'. So the meaning is already symbolic in the Drupal 7 way of addressing this.

I am pretty sure that there hasn't been any testing done without any CSS, I do wonder what other errors we'll catch by doing so. I do wonder though if perhaps this is an overly generalized guideline. Are people finding this a barrier? Is disabling CSS still relevant? It's probably more common to disable JavaScript, but there's lots that you can't do in any modern system without enabling it.

Are people in D8 theming the required element more now? Would everyone just be as happy if we'd kept it like we did in D7?

comments.author: duaelfr
comments.body_html:
Since screen readers are already using the aria-required and the html5 required attributes to vocalise the mandatory status of the field, anything we may add in the markup should be marked as aria-hidden and speak: none to avoid the noise. Given that, we could just go back to the exact same markup than D7 which used <span class="form-required" title="This field is required.">*</span>. This way, themers could still hide the common star and use CSS to put their own required style. We keep accessibility AND themability.

(IMHO, we should consider to use another class on this span that could be easier to target than this generic one.)

comments.author: duaelfr
comments.body_html:
@mgifford The thing is that screen readers are already translating aria/html5 attributes to something. We need to hide this new string from them in any case to avoid a double indication. To summarize, we would need something like:
<label for="edit-account-name" class="js-form-required form-required">Username<span aria-hidden="true" class="hidden"> (required)<span></label>

Doing this way:

  1. users without screen reader and with CSS won't notice any change (span hidden and :after maintained on the label)
  2. users without screen reader and without CSS are going to see the "(required)" string appended to the label
  3. users with screen reader and with CSS are going to hear the label then the required sentence given by the aria-required attribute of the targetted field but not the content of the span (class hidden => display none)
  4. users with screen reader and without CSS are going to hear the label then the required sentence given by the aria-required attribute of the targetted field but not the content of the span (aria-hidden attribute)

comments.body_html:
#11 is on the right track.

I think it should work well for sighted screen reader users too. With CSS they will see an asterisk, and hear "required". Without CSS they see and hear "required" (in English, anyway).

There might a localization issue here. What if an operating system or screen reader localization announces the required attribute using one phrase, but Drupal localizes "required" as a different phrase? Like the difference between "mandatory" and "compulsory". I've never used a screen reader in any language other than English, so I don't know. It's beyond our control though.

A minor point: the span doesn't need to be inside the label - it won't form part of the accessible name for assistive tech either way. For all the scenarios in #11, the following pattern also works:

<label for="edit-account-name" class="js-form-required form-required">Username</label><span aria-hidden="true" class="hidden"> (required)<span>

The difference between the two is that in #11 the word required is clickable, but in this version it isn't clickable.

comments.author: andrewmacpherson
comments.body_html:
Re: #23 and #24 - This is about avoiding verbosity in assistive tech, e.g. screen readers announcing "required" twice. The use of aria-hidden="true" is sufficient to ensure that span is hidden from AT, regardless of whether author CSS gets applied or not. So in this sense it doesn't really matter whether we use .hidden or .visually-hidden.

I think we should stick with .hidden for a couple of reasons:

  1. .hidden will effectively hide it from legacy browser/AT combinations which don't support aria-hidden, but .visually-hidden won't.
  2. .hidden is a much simpler (safer) implementation than .visually-hidden. It just uses display:none instead of all the properties needed for the 1px clip technique. Note that the .visually-hidden CSS itself needs ongoing review for nest practice. (See #2819823: CSS clip deprecated - .visually-hidden needs an update?.)

comments.body_html:
ok after quite a few discussions with @kentr and @mgifford we came up with the following approach. first a bit of context. this issue would be ready to go. problem is due to the introduction of the fix for removing the start from the aural interface based on my suggestion in https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/12981/diffs?c... this issue would be blocked by #2852874: [Meta] Set the required state for all fields in Core in the Accessibility Object Model (AOM). by removing the star fields that dont have a programmatic required label would be unidentifiable for screenreader users. :( and it turned out in my testing that not only the field is missing the required attribute but also:

  • timestamp
  • formatted text long
  • formatted text long sum
  • image
  • comment

so our consensus was the following:

  • revert this commit https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/12981/diffs?c... on this MR. after that this issue looks good and ready for RTBC. the sooner the better it gets in.
  • the changes from the reverted commit should go into the following issue instead #3568100: [PP-1] Avoid the announcement of the star for required fields in the aural interface. i've already outlined the necessary changes made on the issue and also noted to credit @duaelFr. for gin i've also created an issue before introducing the same changes #3566851: [PP-1] Avoid announcing the star for required fields in the aural interface .
  • Both issues are postponed now on #2852874: [Meta] Set the required state for all fields in Core in the Accessibility Object Model (AOM), and the scope of that issue is getting expanded not only adding a required attribute to the file field but also to all other fields in core that are missing a required attribute.

so to summarize the sole step relevant for the current issue is roll back https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/merge_requests/12981/diffs?c... , do a last recheck, finish the change record, and then this issue should be ready for RTBC imho- apologies for the back and forth :(

comments.author: kentr
comments.body_html:
Other concerns:

1. Regarding fieldset (#104 #107) and the file and image fields in the screenshots

Currently, in Claro, those aren't fieldset elements. They're details / summary elements.

However, the MR does add the "(required)" text for fieldset elements.

So the question is, do we actually want that for fieldset elements? Because actual labels for individual fields also have "(required)".

I'm seeing this also on required Datetime fields in the Stark theme, which uses the base system template that arbitrary themes might use if they don't override it.

2. Regarding datetime-wrapper.html.twig

Per #111, several instances of datetime-wrapper.html.twig are modified.

These changes are evident with required Timestamp fields, again in Stark theme.

To me, the change creates a problem. It adds the "(required)" text to h4 elements above the actual input fields, and the fields themselves also have "(required)". So, my thought is that datetime-wrapper.html.twig should not be modified for this issue.

What are thoughts on these points?

[edited to fix typos & improve formatting]

comments.author: kentr
comments.body_html:
I don't mean to rock the boat, but now that I've seen a mechanism for appending text to labels / names without modifying templates, I'm wondering if that's a better approach.

Adding the '(required)' text in templates means that existing sites with custom templates have to update their templates, and also carries the risk that it will get accidentally removed from custom templates during their lifespan.

As an alternative, it may be possible to add the text in a ::preRender(), similar to how it is done for #2848507: Indicate that grouping elements have child element errors for ux and a11y:

$element['#title'] = new TranslatableMarkup('@title <span class="visually-hidden child-error-indicator">(contains error)</span>', ['@title' => $element['#title']]);

I also wonder if translating the full string like this instead of just the '(required)' text by itself yields a better translation result for some languages.

I'm curious to hear others' opinions.
